paragraphs.text: Class and job are informal terms for creature types that describe what a creature does, such as Rogue , Soldier , or Wizard . These contrast with species creature types, which describe what a creature is (e.g. Human or Goblin ).

Most humanoid creatures have at least two creature types : a species and a class. Whereas species (such as Human , Elf , or Goblin ) is a matter of the creature's origin, their class (such as Soldier , Wizard , or Rogue ) represents their function, occupation, career, or calling in life.

There is no distinction in the Comprehensive Rules between species and class. All creature types are treated equally within the game rules. The use of the species/class model is to allow for more consistent, flavorful worldbuilding and more design space among creatures.
Some cards, including a few tokens , can have a class without a species. There are currently 69 cards with only a class type.
As of Jumpstart 2022 the most common class is Wizard, followed by Warrior and then Soldier.
Not all non-species creature types have to be occupations. Types as Child , Coward , Elder , Guest and Peasant are categories you can apply to creatures.

Classes like Cleric , Knight and Wizard have been a part of Magic 's creature types since Limited Edition Alpha . During the early years of the game, creature types were considered to be an extension of the flavor and world-building, rather than as mechanically important. This had two consequences — creatures had only a single creature type and that creature type was the most flavourfully relevant one.

Classes were a major part of R&D's shift away from creature-types-as-flavour to creature-types-as-mechanics. This philosophy change arose from development of the tribal -themed Onslaught block , when three major issues with the current design scheme were identified:
Creatures having only one type meant someone had to choose which type was more important when a creature, like Goblin Wizard , wanted to be multiple types.
With only one creature type, card names were being used to tell the whole story about a card. This limited the name space for creatures.
Creatures with only one type would only work in one type of tribal deck. This limited flexability and interactivity for players.

In response to the success of Onslaught block, the race/class model was adopted for creatures from Mirrodin onwards. The Grand Creature Type Update consolidated the race/class model by reducing the number of creature types and issuing errata to older cards to bring them in line with the new philosophy.

In 2022 Wizards of the Coast retired the silver border , replacing it with the acorn stamp. This allowed Un-sets to contain both acorn cards and eternal-legal cards. The release of Unfinity saw Child and Gamer become eternal legal classes.

Playtest cards use creature types which are not included in Magic 's comprehensive rules, but are part of Chaos Draft , Unknown Event , or other casual games. Because these creature types are not compiled into an authoritative list by Wizards of the Coast , the following table may be incomplete. Which of the playtest card creature types are considered classes is based on intuition rather than official comment.

During the Grand Creature Type Update, a number of classes were made obsolete. They were removed from the comprehensive rules list of types and the cards that previously bore them were issued with errata that replaced those types.
Since the update, some of the obsolete classes have be brought back into use. This table only lists creature types that have stayed obsolete and not brought back.
Being obsolete is not the same as being retired, which only means R&D will stop making new cards using the retired creature type.
